definition.text: This repo's own target architecture draws three memory kinds, not the two this card's name implies: working memory ("working memory - what one run is currently holding in context, including its compaction transitions"), episodic memory ("episodic memory - what happened in earlier runs, retrievable and expirable"), and long-term memory ("long-term memory - durable claims about the world, superseded rather than edited"). The short/long-term split this card's own name uses maps onto their declared lifetimes: working memory is scoped to a single run, while episodic and long-term memory are declared to last indefinitely -- a lifetime distinction, not merely a content distinction.

evidence.quote: working memory - what one run is currently holding in context, including its compaction transitions
episodic memory - what happened in earlier runs, retrievable and expirable
long-term memory - durable claims about the world, superseded rather than edited

landscape.text: 2026 practice has shifted from pre-indexing everything into an embedding store toward just-in-time / agentic retrieval: "agents built with the 'just in time' approach maintain lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, web links, etc.) and use these references to dynamically load data into context at runtime using tools" -- trading query-time latency for avoiding a stale index. Several production coding agents are named as having already dropped pre-indexed vector search in favor of this pattern. Staleness is a measured problem for the pre-indexed approach specifically: a June 2026 paper finds plain similarity-ranked retrieval "serves superseded values 15-40% of the time", which a deterministic supersession layer drives toward zero -- direct evidence that freshness has to be tracked as metadata, not inferred from an embedding. Separately, no standard interface exists across vector databases: the same atomic write operation is named differently by every vendor, so a retrieval implementation is not portable the way this repo's other capability interfaces are designed to be.

evidence.quote: agents built with the 'just in time' approach maintain lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, web links, etc.) and use these references to dynamically load data into context at runtime using tools.

By 2026, systems like Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and others no longer index their target corpora into a vector database, instead exposing retrieval as a set of tools and letting the LLM decide what to call, when, and how often.
RAG serves superseded values 15-40% of the time; MemStrata drives this to ~0%, a failure class RAG cannot avoid.
the atomic operation of inserting or updating a record is upsert in Pinecone [6], insert in Milvus [7] (with separate upsert for updates) and add or upsert in Chroma [8].

usage.text: A caller reaches two different contracts depending on horizon. Short-term is seam-dispatch's declared context: a request states what context a unit receives and its token ceiling, a result states the summary folded back to the parent, and every compaction is a recorded transition rather than an invisible one -- "Compaction is the practice of taking a conversation nearing the context window limit, summarizing its contents, and reinitiating a new context window with the summary." A unit can also branch a separate working context for an independent sub-task and fold back only the result. Long-term is cap-memory's remember/recall/supersede/forget -- folded whole into cap-state-persistence's own skill file rather than kept as a standalone top-level skill -- where recall takes a scope selector and a need, never an embedding or a similarity threshold; the wider practice this contract follows scopes every search by tagging dimension: "Memory is scoped along four independent dimensions: user (user_id), agent (agent_id), app (app_id), and session/run (run_id), which are tagging dimensions, not nested layers."

evidence.quote: Compaction is the practice of taking a conversation nearing the context window limit, summarizing its contents, and reinitiating a new context window with the summary.
An agent can procedurally branch into a sub-trajectory to handle a subtask and then fold it upon completion, collapsing the intermediate steps while retaining a concise summary of the outcome.
Memory is scoped along four independent dimensions: user (user_id), agent (agent_id), app (app_id), and session/run (run_id), which are tagging dimensions, not nested layers.

gaps.what: Whether cap-state-persistence's memory-item claim is genuine coverage or a naming coincidence, resolved: it is genuine. cap-state-persistence's skill.json folds a complete former "cap-memory" skill whole -- its own purpose, contract (remember/recall/supersede/forget), MemoryItem shape, and its own harness at harness/memory -- not a passing mention. But cap-memory has no standalone top-level skill directory (there is no `.claude/skills/cap-memory`; it lives only as a `folded` sub-object inside `cap-state-persistence/skill.json`), so a reader browsing the skill-layer listing alone would never find it.
gaps.why_it_matters: A card whose real owner is a folded sub-skill rather than a top-level one is easy to miss when auditing which skill backs which card.
gaps.research_query: should cap-memory be un-folded back into its own top-level skill directory now that this card treats it as a first-class element?

gaps.what: All three architecture entities this card's name maps to -- A-state-working-memory, A-state-episodic-memory, A-state-long-term-memory -- carry status "gap" and home_today "gap" in the architecture blueprint: even this repo's own target design has not assigned any of the three a running home today.
gaps.why_it_matters: This directly undercuts the "built" status this card carries in the reference model; none of the three memory kinds this card defines has a claimed-running implementation, only a proposed contract.
gaps.research_query: does harness/memory's dryrun adapter actually exercise all three memory kinds (working, episodic, long-term), or only the recall/supersede/forget shape that maps to episodic and long-term?

gaps.what: No ratified standard exists for agent memory (per this repo's own architecture entity, sourced to research and to PASS.md). The Model Context Protocol's Resources primitive is the closest cross-vendor mechanism touching retrieval, but it defines only generic resource discovery/read (a URI, a mimeType, a lastModified timestamp) -- no query field, similarity score, ranked-result-set schema, or corpus-description schema -- so it does not actually govern memory or retrieval.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without a standard, this card's own proposed MemoryItem shape and scope grammar are this repo's design alone, not an adoption of external convention, the same status this repo gives durable execution and state persistence generally.
gaps.research_query: is any working group extending MCP Resources (or a competing protocol) toward a retrieval-specific request/result schema?

gaps.what: The seam this card draws against the shared Knowledge service (base.3) -- working memory run-scoped and homed in seam-dispatch, versus long-term memory forever-lived and scoped per-principal via cap-memory -- is reasoned from this repo's own target architecture and research, not checked against a real running Knowledge service on the other side: base.3 itself carries status "planned" in the reference model and has no card profile written yet.
gaps.why_it_matters: The distinction this profile draws (lifetime and per-principal scope, not content) is a real seam claim if base.3 is ever built the way TARGET describes it, but it is currently argued rather than measured against an actual counterpart.
gaps.research_query: once base.3 Knowledge has a card profile, does its own evidence describe scoping and lifetime the same way, or does it assume a single shared, unscoped corpus?

gaps.what: This repo's own retrieval tooling (tools/kb_index.py, which builds one pre-indexed lexical corpus written to docs/reference/kb-index.json, plus tools/kb.py show, which resolves one record by id at call time) does not cleanly sit on either side of the sourced just-in-time-vs-pre-indexed tradeoff above: it pre-builds an index (the older pattern) but the index is lexical, not embedding-based, and it also supports call-time id resolution (the newer pattern).
gaps.why_it_matters: The landscape tradeoff sourced above is drawn entirely from third-party evidence about other systems; this repo's own retrieval tool is neither confirming nor disconfirming evidence for it, and no research record documents this repo's own tool this way.
gaps.research_query: none -- this is an observation about this repo's own code, not a claim requiring further sourcing

gaps.what: Several tools citations here rest on search-only or fetch-refused records: X-refmodel-base-3-knowledge-003's page fetch was refused (HTTP 403), and -005/-006 have no independently recovered publish date, consistent with this repo's standing limit that page fetch is blocked in this environment (STATUS rows 14, 45). Named customer/adoption figures (Bazaarvoice, Kakao, BIGO, the 44,000 GitHub-star count) are carried from search-result snippets, not verified against the cited articles' own sources.
gaps.why_it_matters: The vendor landscape in this card rests on secondary reporting about adoption, not primary verification; a named customer claim could be marketing copy rather than a checkable fact.
gaps.research_query: capture the underlying vendor comparison articles with tools/capture.py to get verbatim, source-checked adoption figures
